newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Colombo port gets tough in bid to raise efficiency.
newsitem.headline: Colombo port gets tough in bid to raise efficiency.

text.p: Colombo port has cracked down on labour and plans new tariffs to improve services and attract bigger and more modern vessels, industry officials said on Monday.

"The need for improvement in productivity is definitely there," Faizer Hashim, chairman of the Ceylon Association of Ships' Agents (CASA), told Reuters. "The port must run itself as a more commercially-oriented place."

Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) officials said they faced mounting complaints of delays. Ships were using rival ports such as Singapore because of the poor service at Colombo, south Asia's trans-shipment hub, they said.

The SLPA runs Colombo, which last year handled just over one million containers and has a capacity of 1.6 million containers. Trans-shipment traffic accounts for about 70 percent of the number of containers handled by the port.

Colombo handles about 23 percent of cargo from the Indian subcontinent but faces stiff competition from ports such as Singapore as cargo volumes increase with the liberalisation of India's economy, port officials say.

SLPA spokesman Daya Wijesekera said the port would impose tough penalties and improve a 30-year-old incentive scheme to raise labour productivity. It would also increase private labour to handle "dirty cargo", such as cement and fertilizer.

A recent study on productivity found that attendance of workers in the port's operations division was unsatisfactory and that attendance on Mondays and Tuesday was as low as 50 percent, Wijesekera said.
"More than anything else, there's the need to discipline labour," CASA's Hashim said. "We've been crying for it."
The SLPA plans to build a dormitory for up to 1,000 workers following complaints that inadequate public transport and accommodation contributed to poor attendance, Wijesekera said.
It would also improve transport inside the port and reopen gates closed because of security problems, he said.
Security was tightened after Tamil Tiger rebels, fighting for independence for minority Tamils in this Indian Ocean island's north and east, staged an abortive suicide attack on the port in April.

SLPA officials said they planned to standardised the port's tariff structure for conventional cargo under which tariffs paid by shipping lines will depend on daily output, with higher output reducing the charge and vice versa.

"We're looking at productivity-based tariffs," a senior SLPA official said. "If a ship does more cargo she pays less. By doing this we want to encourage vessels handling large volumes and with modern equipment that will give faster turnaround times which eventually will reduce costs."
Until now, tariffs were imposed on cargo movement regardless of output levels, he said.
The port made no profit from conventional cargo such as grain and cement and tariffs had not been revised since 1982 although costs such as fuel and salaries had gone up, he said.
CASA's Hashim said the port should improve its services before raising tariffs on conventional cargo.
